Our library changed its hours last winter. On the first Monday of the new schedule, I arrived after work and found four people waiting outside. The lights were on, but the door was locked. A small notice explained that the evening shift had been cancelled because few visitors had used it in September. That answer bothered me. September is the month when the college library is still open late, and our branch is close to the college. The month the council counted may have been the one month it should have ignored.

I asked the librarian what an evening shift cost. She did not have the figure, but she showed me where to read the council minutes. The minutes listed salaries for the entire library system. They said nothing about our branch. At the next public meeting, I asked whether the council had considered keeping one late evening instead of three. One member said it would be confusing. Another asked what day we would choose. Friday seemed obvious to me until a parent pointed out that her family needed the room on Tuesdays, when her son had a lesson nearby.

We finally agreed to count visitors for six weeks, on two different evenings. I took a turn counting on a rainy Tuesday. Only seven people came in. One stayed for two hours, filling out forms on a library computer. The tally did not explain why that visit mattered. In my notes I wrote the time he left, so I would remember it when we looked at the numbers.
